unit.title: The Book and How We Got It
unit.summary: Before we ask how to read the Bible, we ask what it is and where it came from. This unit follows the Bible from events and spoken memories to written scrolls, from scrolls to collections and a recognised canon, from hand-copied manuscripts to the printed and translated Bibles we hold today, in English and in Tamil. Along the way it asks what the Bible is for, why so many voices over so many centuries tell one story, what the manuscript differences really change, and what is gained and lost when God's word crosses from Hebrew and Greek into our own languages.

lessons.title: Why the Bible?
lessons.question: Why do we have a Bible at all, what is it for, and how can so many writers over so many centuries tell one story?
lessons.bigIdea: The Bible is God's gift of a shared memory: a library written by about 40 people over roughly 1,500 years, not written to us but given to us, so that we might know the God who has finally shown his face in Jesus. Scripture bears witness to the Word; it is not a rule book for its own sake.

sections.heading: A library, not a single book
sections.body:
The word 'Bible' comes from the Greek *ta biblia*, which means 'the books'. That plural is a good place to start. The Bible is a library: 66 books in most Protestant Bibles, more in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles (Lesson 2 explains why). It holds stories, laws, songs, proverbs, prophetic poems, letters, biographies of Jesus and visions.

The two halves are called 'Testaments'. A testament here means a covenant: a binding, relational agreement. The Old Testament tells of God's covenant with Israel. The New Testament tells of the new covenant made through Jesus, which the prophets had promised (Jer 31:31-34; Luke 22:20). So from the start the Bible is not a list of rules floating in the air. It is the record of a relationship.

Jesus himself named the Scriptures of his day by their three parts: 'the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms' (Luke 24:44). Jewish readers still call this collection the *Tanakh*, from the first letters of Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).

sections.heading: Why write anything down?
sections.body:
God speaks because he wants to be known. People forget, so God's acts were written down as a memorial. After the battle with Amalek, Moses is told to 'write this in a book as a memorial' (Exod 17:14). The book of the law was placed beside the ark as a witness (Deut 31:24-26). Habakkuk is told to write the vision plainly on tablets so that a runner may read it (Hab 2:2).

The New Testament gives its own reasons. John says his Gospel was written 'so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name' (John 20:31). John's first letter says the apostles write what they have seen and touched so that readers may share their fellowship 'with the Father and with his Son' (1 John 1:1-4). Paul says the older Scriptures were written 'for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope' (Rom 15:4).

So the purpose is relational: life, fellowship, hope, and being made 'wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus' and equipped for good work (2 Tim 3:15-17). Jesus warned against missing that purpose. Some people searched the Scriptures carefully but would not come to him, the one the Scriptures pointed to (John 5:39-40).

sections.heading: Not written to us, but given to us
sections.body:
Every book of the Bible had a first audience. Paul's letter to the Corinthians is addressed 'to the church of God that is in Corinth' (1 Cor 1:2), and the letter to the Galatians 'to the churches of Galatia' (Gal 1:2). When Paul asks Timothy to bring the cloak he left at Troas (2 Tim 4:13), he is not asking you to bring a cloak. Old Testament scholar John Walton often puts it this way: the Bible was written *for* us, but it was not written *to* us.

This is not a way of making the Bible less important. It is a way of honouring how God actually gave it. We are like people reading someone else's letters, which God has deliberately handed to us. Paul says the stories of Israel 'were written down for our instruction' (1 Cor 10:11). They were first lived and written by others; then they were given to us.

The practical result is simple. Before asking 'What does this mean for me?', ask 'What did this mean for them?' Then ask how God's purpose for them, now fulfilled and clarified in Jesus, speaks to us. Lesson 12 on culture, date and audience develops this in detail.

sections.heading: Forty voices, one story
sections.body:
The Bible was written by about 40 authors over roughly 1,500 years. (The learner's notes say 1,000 years; on the traditional dating the span is longer, from Moses around 1400 BC to the book of Revelation around AD 95.) Many critical scholars date much of the Old Testament later, so on their view most of the writing falls within about 1,000 years. Either way it is a very long time. The writers include a shepherd-king, priests, prophets, fishermen, a tax collector, a doctor and a tentmaker. They wrote in three languages (Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek) and in places from Babylon to Rome.

Yet these voices tell one story. God creates a good world (Gen 1:31). Humans turn away and the world is broken (Gen 3). God promises to bless all nations through Abraham (Gen 12:1-3), forms Israel and frees them from slavery (Exod 19:4-6), promises a king from David's line (2 Sam 7:12-16), disciplines and restores them, and then comes himself in Jesus. Jesus taught his disciples to read the whole story this way: 'beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself' (Luke 24:27). The story ends with a renewed creation where God lives with his people (Rev 21:1-5).

Many believers rightly see this unity as a sign of God's hand. It is also honest to say that unity is not sameness. The Bible holds real conversations within itself: Job and Ecclesiastes push back on easy readings of Proverbs, and Chronicles retells Kings with different emphases. The single story is carried by many voices, not one flat voice.

sections.heading: God did not bypass the human authors
sections.body:
The Bible does not describe itself as words dropped from heaven. Luke tells us he researched carefully, used eyewitness reports and wrote an orderly account (Luke 1:1-4). Paul's personality is everywhere: his anger (Gal 5:12), his tears (2 Cor 2:4), even a moment where he cannot quite remember whom he baptised (1 Cor 1:14-16). Jeremiah dictated his words to a human secretary, Baruch (Jer 36:4). Each writer has his own vocabulary and style.

At the same time, the writers spoke from God as they were 'carried along by the Holy Spirit' (2 Pet 1:21). The picture is of a ship carried by the wind: the ship really sails, and the wind really moves it. Inspiration is not dictation. God breathed life through real people, in their own languages, cultures and personalities, and did not switch them off. Unit 2 explores what 'God-breathed' means.

Christians have often compared this to the incarnation. In Jesus, God became fully human without ceasing to be God. In Scripture, God's word comes in fully human words. This is why Hebrews says God spoke 'at many times and in many ways' through the prophets, but has now spoken in his Son, who is the exact imprint of God's nature (Heb 1:1-3). The written words are a true and inspired witness; Jesus is the Word they witness to (John 1:1-18; John 5:39-40).

visuals.title: One story across many books
visuals.intro: Tap each stage of the Bible's story. The arrows show how one stage leads into the next. Notice how every thread runs toward Jesus and on to the new creation.

nodes.label: Good creation
nodes.detail: God makes a good world and gives humans the role of caring for it as his image-bearers.

nodes.label: Turning away
nodes.detail: Humans distrust God and grasp for themselves. Relationships with God, each other and creation break.

nodes.label: Promise to Abraham
nodes.detail: God chooses one family in order to bless every family on earth.

nodes.label: Exodus and covenant
nodes.detail: God frees Israel from slavery and then gives the Law within a covenant relationship.

nodes.label: Kings and prophets
nodes.detail: God promises David a lasting dynasty. Prophets call kings and people back to faithfulness.

nodes.label: Exile and hope
nodes.detail: Israel is exiled to Babylon. The prophets promise a new covenant and a new heart.

nodes.label: Jesus the Messiah
nodes.detail: God comes in person. Jesus lives Israel's story faithfully, dies, rises, and shows what God has always been like.

nodes.label: Spirit and church
nodes.detail: The Spirit is poured out and the good news goes to every nation, as promised to Abraham.

nodes.label: New creation
nodes.detail: God renews heaven and earth and lives with his people. The story ends where it began, but healed.

nodes.label: Scripture as witness
nodes.detail: The written books testify to this story and to the one at its centre.

visuals.title: How do God and the human writers work together?
visuals.intro: Christians agree that God and humans were both involved in writing the Bible. They differ on how. Each position below is held by thoughtful people. Unit 2 looks at these more closely.
visuals.left: God alone (the writer is a pen)

stops.label: Mechanical dictation
stops.who: Some popular piety; rejected by almost all theologians, including the strictest
stops.text: God dictated each word and the writer simply recorded it. Few theologians hold this, because the books plainly show different styles, research and emotions.

stops.label: Verbal plenary inspiration
stops.who: B. B. Warfield, J. I. Packer, the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978)
stops.text: God guided the writers so that every word is what he intended, while using their own personalities and styles. This view explicitly denies dictation.

stops.label: Organic inspiration
stops.who: Herman Bavinck and the Dutch Reformed tradition
stops.text: The Spirit worked through the whole life, culture and character of each writer, like sap through a living tree.

stops.label: True divine and human authors
stops.text: God is the author of Scripture, and the human writers are also true authors who used their own powers. Scripture teaches without error the truth God wanted recorded for our salvation.

stops.label: Incarnational model
stops.text: As Jesus is fully God and fully human, Scripture is fully God's word in fully human, culturally shaped words. Its human marks are not embarrassments but part of how God chose to speak.

stops.label: Witness to the Word, read through Jesus
stops.who: Karl Barth; in a Jesus-centred form Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd
stops.text: Scripture is the inspired witness to God's self-revelation, which is fully given in Jesus. It honestly records God's people's developing perception of him, and Jesus is the lens for reading it.

stops.label: Human religious literature
stops.who: Many secular and liberal critical scholars
stops.text: The Bible is the literature of ancient Israel and the early church, valuable for history and faith, but not inspired in any special sense.

visuals.title: Three ways to hold the Bible
visuals.intro: How you think of the Bible shapes what you look for in it. Compare three common approaches.

rows.label: Main question
cells: What must I do?
What is the answer to my question?
Who is God, what has he done, and who are we in his story?

rows.label: Polygamy in Genesis
cells: Confusing: is it allowed or not?
Look for a verse that settles it.
Reported, not endorsed; the story shows its pain (Gen 29:30-31) and Jesus returns to God's design (Matt 19:4-8).

rows.label: Strength
cells: Takes obedience seriously (John 14:15).
Takes the Bible's truth claims seriously.
Fits the Bible's own shape and Jesus' reading of it (Luke 24:27).

rows.label: Danger
cells: Turns a relationship into a contract; misses genres.
Pulls verses out of their setting.
Can become vague if it ignores clear commands; needs care in defining what is 'Christlike'.

voices.text: Scripture bears witness to the Word; it is not the Word himself (John 5:39–40). Jesus is the measure that measures all.
voices.source: Passage supplied in the learner's course notes
A phrase he has popularised in sermons and books

voices.text: The New is in the Old concealed; the Old is in the New revealed.
voices.source: Popular English rendering of *Questions on the Heptateuch* 2.73 (Latin: Novum in Vetere latet, et in Novo Vetus patet)

views.name: Evangelical: God's written word, fully trustworthy
views.who: J. I. Packer, John Stott, D. A. Carson; the Chicago Statement (1978)
views.summary: The Bible is God's inspired, written word. Because God cannot lie, what Scripture teaches is true and carries God's own authority. It is the final standard for faith and life, and Christians read every part as God's word to his people.
views.strengths: It follows Jesus' own high view of Scripture (Matt 5:18; John 10:35) and gives the church a stable standard that stands above any leader or culture. It takes every book seriously.
views.critiques: Critics say it can treat the Bible as a flat rule book, ignoring genre and the human, historical side. Defenders reply that careful evangelical scholars insist on genre, context and Christ-centred reading.

views.name: Catholic: Scripture within the living Tradition
views.summary: Scripture and Sacred Tradition flow from 'the same divine wellspring' and together form one sacred deposit of the word of God. The Church's teaching office (Magisterium) serves the word and interprets it. Scripture has God as its author and the human writers as true authors.
views.strengths: It matches the historical fact that the Bible came to us through the worshipping church, and it guards against every reader becoming his own pope.
views.critiques: Protestants worry that Tradition and church authority can end up standing over Scripture rather than under it. Catholics reply that the Magisterium is 'not above the word of God, but serves it' (*Dei Verbum* 10).

views.name: Orthodox: Scripture as the heart of Holy Tradition
views.who: Georges Florovsky; Kallistos Ware, *The Orthodox Church*
views.summary: The Bible is the supreme expression of God's revelation, but it lives inside the church's worship, prayer and the writings of the Fathers. It is read, sung and prayed in the liturgy more than studied alone.
views.strengths: It keeps Scripture tied to worship and the community, and it draws deeply on early Christian reading.
views.critiques: Others ask how Tradition can correct itself if Scripture is always read through it. Orthodox reply that the Spirit guides the whole church, not single readers or single councils.

views.name: Jesus-centred: Scripture as witness to the living Word
views.who: Karl Barth (older form); Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Peter Enns, Bill Johnson ('Jesus is perfect theology')
views.summary: The written words are inspired and true witnesses, but the Word of God in the fullest sense is Jesus (John 1:1-18). God spoke partially through the prophets and fully in the Son, the exact imprint of his nature (Heb 1:1-3). So the whole Bible is read with Jesus as its key and goal (John 5:39-40; Luke 24:27).
views.strengths: It follows how the New Testament itself presents Jesus as the climax of revelation, and it keeps Bible study from becoming detached from knowing God. It guards against using verses to justify violence.
views.critiques: Critics warn of a slide toward Marcion (who rejected the Old Testament), note that Jesus himself fully affirmed the Old Testament (Matt 5:17-18) and spoke of judgement, and ask who decides what is 'Christlike'. Defenders reply that they keep the whole Old Testament as inspired and read the Jesus of all four Gospels, including his warnings.

views.name: Jewish: the Tanakh as Israel's covenant library
views.who: Jon Levenson; Adele Berlin and Marc Brettler (eds), *The Jewish Study Bible*
views.summary: The Hebrew Bible is the treasured record of God's covenant with Israel, read together with the Oral Torah and centuries of rabbinic discussion. Its centre is Torah and the ongoing life of the covenant people, not a coming Messiah who has already arrived.
views.strengths: It reminds Christians that these Scriptures belonged to Israel first and that their first meaning matters. Jesus and the apostles were Jewish readers.
views.critiques: Christians read the same texts as finding their fulfilment in Jesus (Luke 24:44). Jewish readers answer that the Christian reading often overlooks the plain meaning for its first audience.

misreadings.topic: The Bible as an owner's manual
misreadings.popular: The Bible is God's instruction manual for life ('Basic Instructions Before Leaving Earth'). Every page tells us what to do, and if something is in the Bible, God approves of it.
misreadings.inContext: Most of the Bible is story, poetry and letters, set inside a covenant relationship. Even the Ten Commandments begin with a rescue: 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt' (Exod 20:2). Much of the narrative reports what happened without approving it: Jacob's two wives bring rivalry and pain (Gen 29:30-31), and kings are told not to multiply wives (Deut 17:17). Scholars such as Gordon Fee, Douglas Stuart and Christopher Wright stress reading each genre as the kind of writing it is.
misreadings.defence: Traditional scholars agree the Bible is not a manual, but they add that it truly does command, and that love for Jesus is shown in keeping his commands (John 14:15). Narrative also teaches, so the answer is not to treat stories as optional but to ask what they teach in context.
misreadings.whyItMatters: A manual reading can make violence or polygamy look approved because they appear in the text. A covenant-story reading asks what God was doing with these people and where the story is heading.

misreadings.topic: Every promise is addressed to me personally
misreadings.popular: Jeremiah 29:11 ('I know the plans I have for you') is God's personal promise that my career, health or relationships will go well.
misreadings.inContext: Jeremiah wrote this to Jewish exiles in Babylon, telling them to settle down because the return would come only after seventy years (Jer 29:10). The 'you' is plural: the whole people. Many who first heard it would die in exile before the promise was fulfilled. Scholars such as John Walton and Christopher Wright point out that the promise is about God's faithfulness to his people over generations.
misreadings.defence: Careful traditional scholars note that the God who kept that promise is unchanging, and Paul says all God's promises find their 'yes' in Christ (2 Cor 1:20). So believers may draw real hope from the verse, as long as they hear it first as a word to a community in exile.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Reading it as a personal guarantee can crush people when life goes badly. Reading it in context gives a deeper hope: God stays faithful to his people even through long, painful seasons.

discuss: Before this lesson, how would you have described what the Bible is? Rule book, love letter, history, something else?
What changes when you read a letter of Paul as someone else's mail that God has handed to you?
Which seems more remarkable to you: that about 40 writers tell one story, or that the story keeps its different voices and tensions? Why?
Jesus said some people searched the Scriptures but would not come to him (John 5:39-40). How can Bible study miss Jesus today?
If God did not bypass the human writers, what does that mean for how we read Paul's emotions or Luke's research?
practice: Read Luke 24:13-35 slowly. Note every phrase about Scripture and every phrase about recognising Jesus. How are the two connected?
Pick a short letter (Philippians or 1 Thessalonians). Before reading, write down who it was written to and what they were going through. Then read it as their mail.
Draw the Bible's story as a simple line with seven points (creation, fall, Abraham, Israel, Jesus, church, new creation). Place three of your favourite passages on it.

lessons.title: How the Bible Was Formed
lessons.question: How did events, memories and writings become one Bible, and who decided which books belong in it?
lessons.bigIdea: The Bible grew in stages: God acted, people remembered and retold, writers wrote, communities copied and collected, and over centuries the church recognised the books it had already been living by. The councils did not create the canon; they recognised it.

sections.heading: First the events, then the memories
sections.body:
Before there was a Bible there were events: a family called out of Mesopotamia, slaves freed from Egypt, a man from Nazareth crucified and raised. The first response was not writing but remembering out loud. After the Red Sea crossing, Moses and Miriam sang (Exod 15:1-21). Parents were told to explain the story when their children asked what the commandments meant (Deut 6:20-25).

This is called *oral tradition*: teaching passed on by speaking, singing and repeating, usually in a community that cares about getting it right. Ancient people trained their memories in ways most of us never do. Paul quotes an early summary of the gospel that he 'received' and 'delivered', two words used for handing on a tradition carefully (1 Cor 15:3-8). Luke says the accounts of Jesus were 'delivered to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word' (Luke 1:1-2).

Oral tradition is not a game of whispers. Scholars such as Richard Bauckham argue that eyewitnesses stayed active in the early churches and acted as a check on the stories. Others think more change happened in the retelling. How much the tradition was controlled is debated, but nearly all agree that the gospel was preached for some decades before the Gospels were written.

sections.heading: From memory to writing
sections.body:
The Bible itself shows writing happening. Moses 'wrote down all the words of the LORD' (Exod 24:4). Joshua wrote in 'the Book of the Law of God' (Josh 24:26). Isaiah's teaching was sealed among his disciples (Isa 8:16), and Jeremiah dictated his messages to Baruch, rewriting the scroll after the king burned it (Jer 36:1-32). King Hezekiah's officials copied out proverbs of Solomon (Prov 25:1).

The writers also used earlier sources, and sometimes name them: the Book of Jashar (Josh 10:13), the Book of the Wars of the LORD (Num 21:14) and royal chronicles (1 Kgs 14:19). These books are lost, but the Bible's authors drew on them. In the New Testament, Paul's letters were written from about AD 50 and passed between churches (Col 4:16). The Gospels followed, most scholars think between about AD 65 and 95.

How long the writing and editing took is debated. Traditional Jewish and Christian belief holds that Moses wrote the Torah in substance. Many critical scholars think the Torah and the historical books were shaped by several sources and editors over centuries, reaching their final form during or after the exile. Many evangelical scholars accept some later editing (Deut 34 records Moses' death) while holding that the core goes back to Moses. Either way, God was at work in the whole process, not only at a single moment of writing.

sections.heading: Collecting the Old Testament
sections.body:
Writings became a collection as God's people used them. When a 'Book of the Law' was found in the temple in King Josiah's day, it led to national repentance (2 Kgs 22:8-13). After the exile, Ezra read the Law aloud to the whole people while Levites explained its sense (Neh 8:1-8). By Jesus' time the Scriptures were known in three parts, the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms or Writings (Luke 24:44). Around AD 95 the Jewish historian Josephus described a fixed set of 22 books (counting several together), which most scholars match to the 39 books of the Protestant Old Testament.

The word *canon* comes from the Greek *kanōn*, a measuring rod. It came to mean the list of books the community measures its faith by. Jews call their canon the Tanakh and count 24 books; Protestants divide the same content into 39.

There is a real difference between churches here. Greek-speaking Jews used the Septuagint, a translation that also included books such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach and 1 and 2 Maccabees. The early church mostly read the Septuagint, so these books were widely read. Catholics call them *deuterocanonical* ('second canon') and confirmed them at the Council of Trent in 1546. The Orthodox churches include them and a few more. Protestants, following the Hebrew canon, call them the Apocrypha: Luther printed them between the Testaments as 'useful and good to read' but not equal to Scripture. See the Canon page for book-by-book detail.

sections.heading: Collecting the New Testament
sections.body:
The first Christians already had a Bible: the Old Testament. Alongside it they treasured the words of Jesus and the teaching of the apostles (2 Thess 2:15; 1 Thess 2:13). Very early, apostolic writings began to be treated as Scripture. Second Peter places Paul's letters alongside 'the other Scriptures' (2 Pet 3:15-16). First Timothy quotes Deuteronomy and a saying found in Luke together, calling both 'Scripture' (1 Tim 5:18; Deut 25:4; Luke 10:7).

In the second century, a teacher named Marcion (around 144) rejected the Old Testament and kept only an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul. Partly in response, church leaders said more clearly which books they had received. Irenaeus (around 180) insisted there are four Gospels, no more and no fewer (*Against Heresies* 3.11.8). The Muratorian Fragment, usually dated to the late second century (some argue for the fourth), lists most of our New Testament.

Some books took longer. Eusebius (around 325) recorded that Hebrews, James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John and Revelation were still questioned in some places (*Church History* 3.25). In 367 Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, gave the first known list of exactly our 27 books. The regional councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) confirmed the same list for their churches.

sections.heading: Recognised, not created
sections.body:
The early church used several tests when weighing a book. Did it come from an apostle or someone close to one (*apostolicity*)? Did it agree with the faith handed down, sometimes called the 'rule of faith' (*orthodoxy*; see Gal 1:8-9)? Was it read widely in worship across the churches (*catholicity*, meaning 'universal')? Was it old enough to come from the apostolic age (*antiquity*)?

The councils did not vote books into holiness. They recognised which books the churches had already been reading and living by, the way a court might recognise someone as a citizen rather than make them one. Protestant scholars such as Michael Kruger stress that the books carried their own authority, which God's people heard. Catholic and Orthodox Christians agree the books were inspired before any council, but stress that the Spirit-led church needed to define the list with authority.

It is also honest to say the process was long and human. Some books were debated for centuries, the edges of the Old Testament still differ between churches, and books like the *Gospel of Thomas* were known but not widely read in worship. Many Christians see in this slow, communal process the same pattern as Lesson 1: God working through people, not around them.

visuals.title: From event to canon
visuals.intro: Step through the stages by which God's acts became the Bible we hold.

steps.label: God acts in history
steps.detail: The exodus, the exile and return, the life, death and resurrection of Jesus. The Bible's starting point is events, not ideas.

steps.label: People remember aloud
steps.detail: Songs, stories, sayings and creeds are passed on carefully by communities and eyewitnesses.

steps.label: Writers write it down
steps.detail: Prophets, scribes, apostles and their helpers write, often using earlier sources and research.

steps.label: Copied and shared
steps.detail: Scrolls and letters are copied and passed between communities and churches.

steps.label: Collected in use
steps.detail: Writings read in worship gather into collections: Law, Prophets, Writings; Gospels and Paul's letters.

steps.label: Recognised as canon
steps.detail: Over centuries the church recognises which books are its measuring rod for faith. Councils confirm what is already widely received.

visuals.title: How the Bible took shape
visuals.intro: Dates before about 600 BC are approximate, and some depend on debated datings of the books.

events.label: Moses (traditional dating)
events.text: Traditional dating for Moses and the giving of the Law. Many scholars prefer a 13th-century exodus, and critical scholars date the Torah's final form much later.

events.label: David and the Psalms
events.text: Songs of worship are written and gathered at Jerusalem.

events.label: Prophets write
events.text: Amos, Hosea, Isaiah and Micah's messages are written down by them or their disciples.

events.label: Book of the Law found
events.text: Josiah's reform after a law scroll is found in the temple.

events.label: Exile to Babylon
events.text: Jerusalem falls. In exile, many scholars think the history and prophets were collected and edited.

events.label: Ezra reads the Law
events.text: The Law is read and explained to the returned community.

events.label: Septuagint begun
events.text: The Torah is translated into Greek in Alexandria; the rest follows over the next two centuries.

events.label: Paul's first letters
events.text: 1 Thessalonians and Galatians are among the earliest New Testament writings.

events.label: Gospels written
events.text: Mark is usually dated around 65-70; Matthew, Luke and John follow by about 95.

events.label: Revelation; Josephus
events.text: The last New Testament book, on most datings. Josephus describes a fixed Jewish canon of 22 books.

events.label: Marcion
events.text: Marcion rejects the Old Testament and edits his own short canon, prompting the church to clarify its own.

events.label: Irenaeus: four Gospels
events.text: Irenaeus defends exactly four Gospels. The Muratorian Fragment may date from about this time.

events.label: Eusebius' categories
events.text: Eusebius records which books are accepted everywhere and which are still disputed.

events.label: Athanasius' list
events.text: The first known list of exactly the 27 New Testament books.

events.label: Council of Carthage
events.text: Following Hippo (393), it confirms the same New Testament list for the African churches.

events.label: Council of Trent
events.text: The Catholic Church formally defines its canon, including the deuterocanonical books, in response to the Reformation.

visuals.title: One Bible, several canons
visuals.intro: All Christians share the same 27 New Testament books. The Old Testament differs. Counts vary by how books are divided.

None

Useful to read but not a source of doctrine (Anglican Article VI)

Tobit, Judith, 1-2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, additions to Esther and Daniel

rows.label: Eastern Orthodox
cells: About 49-51 books, varying by church
The Catholic list plus e.g. 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, Psalm 151, Prayer of Manasseh
Anagignoskomena ('books to be read'): honoured and read; exact status discussed

rows.label: Ethiopian Orthodox
cells: The largest Old Testament
Also 1 Enoch and Jubilees, among others
Canon; 81 books in all on the usual count

voices.text: These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness.
voices.source: *Festal Letter* 39 (AD 367), in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation

views.name: Protestant: a self-authenticating canon, recognised by the church
views.who: F. F. Bruce, *The Canon of Scripture*; Michael J. Kruger, *Canon Revisited*; Herman Ridderbos
views.summary: The canon is the collection of books God inspired. The church did not give them authority; it heard Christ's voice in them and recognised them (John 10:27). Protestants follow the Hebrew Old Testament, the Bible Jesus and the apostles cite, and treat the Apocrypha as useful but not Scripture.
views.strengths: It keeps Scripture above the church and fits the evidence that most books were received widely long before any council.
views.critiques: Catholics and Orthodox ask how a list of books can be known without the church's authority, and note that early Christians widely read the deuterocanonical books. Protestants reply that the church witnesses to the canon without being its source.

views.name: Catholic: the Church defines what it has received
views.who: Council of Trent (1546); *Dei Verbum* 8; Catholic biblical scholars such as Raymond Brown
views.summary: The books are inspired by God, and through Tradition the Church came to know the full list. The Church's authority was needed to define the canon, including the deuterocanonical books that the early church read in the Septuagint.
views.strengths: It matches the historical role of bishops, councils and liturgy, and it explains why many early Christians used the wider Greek Old Testament.
views.critiques: Protestants note that Jewish leaders, Jerome and some early Fathers distinguished these books from the Hebrew canon, and that a formal Catholic definition came only in 1546.

views.name: Orthodox: a living canon within Tradition
views.who: Eastern Orthodox churches; the Synod of Jerusalem (1672); Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church
views.summary: The canon is received in the church's worship. The core is fixed, but the edges are held with less legal precision. Extra books are read and honoured as *anagignoskomena*, and some churches, like the Ethiopian, keep a wider list.
views.strengths: It reflects the early church's own practice, where the boundary was settled by long use more than by a single decree.
views.critiques: Others see this as leaving the boundary unclear. Orthodox reply that the church lives by its Scripture in worship, not by legal lists.

views.name: Critical-historical: a long human process
views.who: Lee Martin McDonald, *The Biblical Canon*; Bart D. Ehrman, *Lost Christianities*
views.summary: Canon formation was a gradual, sometimes contested human process, shaped by worship, debates with groups like the Gnostics and Marcion, and the growing power of the mainstream church. Other early writings were read in some places.
views.strengths: It takes the historical evidence of disputes and variety seriously and corrects the idea of a canon dropped from heaven.
views.critiques: Others reply that the core of the New Testament (four Gospels and Paul) was widely received by about 180, long before political power was involved, and that 'alternative' gospels were mostly later and not widely read in worship.

views.name: Jewish: the Tanakh received by Israel
views.who: Rabbinic tradition; Mishnah *Yadayim* 3:5; modern scholars such as Timothy Lim
views.summary: The 24 books of the Tanakh were received over time by the Jewish people. Rabbis later discussed whether books such as Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs belonged, and affirmed that they did.
views.strengths: It is the canon Jesus and the apostles knew, read in its original languages.
views.critiques: Christians note that many first-century Jews also read the wider Greek Scriptures, and that the Christian canon adds the apostolic witness to Jesus.

misreadings.topic: Constantine or the Council of Nicaea chose the books
misreadings.popular: A widespread claim (popularised by novels such as *The Da Vinci Code*) is that Emperor Constantine or the Council of Nicaea in 325 decided which books went into the Bible and suppressed the rest.
misreadings.inContext: Nicaea dealt with the teaching of Arius about Christ and with the date of Easter. It made no decision about the canon. The four Gospels were already defended as a set by Irenaeus around 180, and most of the New Testament was in wide use before Constantine was born. Historians across the spectrum, including Bruce Metzger and the sceptical scholar Bart Ehrman, reject the claim.
misreadings.defence: What the claim gets partly right: Constantine did order fifty Bibles for the churches of Constantinople (Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* 4.36), imperial support helped standardise copies, and the edges of the canon were still being settled in the fourth century.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If people think an emperor invented the Bible, they may distrust it for the wrong reason. The real history is slower, more communal and more interesting.

misreadings.topic: The Council of Jamnia closed the Old Testament around AD 90
misreadings.popular: Older textbooks and sermons often say that a rabbinic 'Council of Jamnia' (Yavneh) around AD 90 officially fixed the Jewish canon.
misreadings.inContext: In 1964 Jack P. Lewis showed that there was no binding council of this kind. The rabbis at Yavneh discussed whether certain books such as Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs 'defile the hands' (were holy), but they were debating books already in use, not closing a list. Many scholars now think the canon was settled mainly by long use.
misreadings.defence: Some scholars, such as Roger Beckwith, argue the Hebrew canon was effectively fixed much earlier (by the second century BC), pointing to Jesus' 'Law, Prophets and Psalms' (Luke 24:44) and Josephus. Others, such as Lee McDonald, think the edges stayed open into the second century AD. Both reject a single closing council.
misreadings.whyItMatters: It shows that canon is mainly about what God's people received and lived by, not a single decision by one meeting.

discuss: Why do you think God chose to work through decades of oral memory and centuries of collecting, rather than handing over a finished book?
Does it trouble you or encourage you that some books, like 2 Peter and Revelation, were debated for a long time? Why?
What is the difference between a council creating a canon and recognising one? Why does it matter?
Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians share the whole New Testament but differ on parts of the Old. How should this shape how we speak about each other?
Which of the four tests (apostolic, orthodox, widely used, ancient) seems most important to you, and why?
practice: Read 1 Corinthians 15:1-11 and mark the words for 'received' and 'delivered'. Write the early creed in your own words.
Read Luke 1:1-4 and list every step Luke describes between the events and his written Gospel.
Open the Canon page in this app and read about one deuterocanonical book you have never read. Note why different churches treat it differently.

lessons.title: Manuscripts, Codices and Variants
lessons.question: We do not have the original pages. So how do we know what the Bible said, and what do the differences between manuscripts really change?
lessons.bigIdea: The original writings are lost, but thousands of copies survive, some very early. Comparing them (textual criticism) lets scholars recover the text with great confidence. The differences are real and worth knowing, but no core Christian belief depends on a disputed reading.

sections.heading: No originals, but a mountain of copies
sections.body:
None of the original documents written by Moses, Isaiah, Paul or John survives. Scholars call the originals *autographs*. What we have are *manuscripts*: copies made by hand, first on papyrus (paper made from reeds) and later on parchment (prepared animal skin). Copying by hand was slow, skilled work, and every copyist could make mistakes.

For the New Testament, over 5,800 Greek manuscripts are catalogued, from tiny scraps to complete Bibles. There are also about 10,000 Latin manuscripts, many in Syriac, Coptic and other ancient languages, and countless quotations in the writings of early Christian teachers. No other ancient book comes close to this number, and few have copies so close in time to when they were written.

For the Old Testament, the standard Hebrew text is the *Masoretic Text*, named after the Masoretes, Jewish scribes who between about AD 600 and 1000 added vowel signs and detailed notes to protect every letter. The oldest complete copy is the Leningrad Codex (1008), the basis of most modern Hebrew Bibles; the Aleppo Codex (about 930) is older but partly lost. The Greek Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls give us much older witnesses.

sections.heading: The Dead Sea Scrolls
sections.body:
In 1947 Bedouin shepherds found jars of scrolls in a cave near Qumran, by the Dead Sea. Over the next decade eleven caves yielded remains of more than 900 manuscripts, copied between about 250 BC and AD 68. Around 230 of them are biblical books. Every book of the Old Testament is represented except Esther.

The most famous is the Great Isaiah Scroll, copied around 125 BC. It is about a thousand years older than the oldest complete Masoretic manuscripts, yet its text agrees closely with them, apart mostly from spelling and small differences. This showed how carefully the Hebrew text had been passed on.

The scrolls also showed that, before the first century, more than one form of some books was in circulation. A Samuel scroll (4QSam-a) often agrees with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text, and a shorter form of Jeremiah matches the Septuagint. A scroll of Deuteronomy reads 'sons of God' at Deut 32:8 where the Masoretic Text reads 'sons of Israel'. Modern translations use this evidence, and their footnotes often say so.

sections.heading: Papyri and the great codices
sections.body:
A *codex* is a book with pages, as opposed to a scroll. Early Christians adopted the codex very quickly, perhaps because it could hold several Gospels or letters together and was easy to carry.

The oldest New Testament pieces are papyri. P52, a fragment the size of a credit card held in Manchester, has a few lines of John 18:31-33 and 18:37-38. It is often dated to around AD 125-175, though some scholars, such as Brent Nongbri, argue that a later date is possible. P46 (around 200) contains most of Paul's letters, P66 (around 200) much of John, and P75 (around 175-225) parts of Luke and John. P75 is remarkably close to Codex Vaticanus, made more than a century later, which shows careful copying.

The great fourth- and fifth-century codices are complete or nearly complete Bibles in Greek. *Codex Vaticanus* (about 300-350) has been in the Vatican Library since at least the 1470s. (The learner's notes call it 'variantas'; the name is Vaticanus.) *Codex Sinaiticus* (about 330-360) was found by Constantin von Tischendorf at St Catherine's Monastery in Sinai in 1844 and 1859; it is the oldest complete New Testament and also contains the *Epistle of Barnabas* and the *Shepherd of Hermas*. Its leaves are now divided between London, Leipzig, Sinai and St Petersburg, and can be viewed online. *Codex Alexandrinus* (early 400s) was given to King Charles I of England in 1627 by Patriarch Cyril Lucaris and is in the British Library.

sections.heading: What a variant is, and three famous ones
sections.body:
A *textual variant* is any place where manuscripts differ. Scholars estimate there are several hundred thousand variants in the New Testament manuscripts, more than the roughly 138,000 words of the Greek New Testament. That sounds alarming, but every difference in every copy is counted. The great majority are spelling, word order (which barely matters in Greek), 'Christ Jesus' versus 'Jesus Christ', or an obvious slip. A small number make a real difference to a verse, and a very few involve whole passages.

The ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20) is missing in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; Vaticanus leaves a blank column after Mark 16:8, as if the scribe knew of something more. Most scholars think Mark originally ended at 16:8 or that the original ending was lost. The resurrection appearances in verses 9-20 are also told in the other Gospels, but the snake-handling and poison-drinking verses (Mark 16:17-18) occur only here.

The woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and appears in different places in later ones, sometimes after Luke 21:38. Many scholars think it is a true early story about Jesus that was added to John later. The 'Johannine Comma' in 1 John 5:7-8 ('the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one'), found in the KJV, appears in no Greek manuscript before the medieval period and entered Erasmus' Greek New Testament only in his 1522 edition. The Trinity does not depend on it: the church confessed the Trinity at Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) without it, from passages such as Matt 28:19 and 2 Cor 13:14.

sections.heading: Textual criticism: weighing the witnesses
sections.body:
*Textual criticism* is the careful comparison of manuscripts to find the earliest form of the text. 'Criticism' here means judgement, not attack. Its main tools are simple to grasp. Manuscripts are weighed, not just counted. Earlier copies usually matter more. The best reading is the one that best explains how the others arose. A harder reading is often older, because scribes tended to smooth difficulties, not create them. Readings found in many regions are stronger than readings found in one.

Manuscripts fall into rough families. The *Alexandrian* (from Egypt: P75, Vaticanus, Sinaiticus) is usually the earliest and most careful. The *Western* (Codex Bezae, Old Latin) is early but freer. The *Byzantine* (most later Greek manuscripts) became the standard text of the Greek church. A *Caesarean* family is now doubted by many scholars.

Erasmus printed the first published Greek New Testament in 1516 from a handful of late Byzantine manuscripts. Its descendants, later called the *Textus Receptus* ('received text'), lay behind the KJV of 1611. Since the 1800s, older manuscripts have changed the picture. Westcott and Hort (1881) judged that only a tiny fraction of the text, around one part in a thousand, was still seriously in doubt. Today the Nestle-Aland (28th edition, 2012) and United Bible Societies editions underlie most modern translations, and newer computer-assisted methods continue the work. Scholars as different as Bruce Metzger and Bart Ehrman agree that the text can be recovered to a very high degree, while still debating how much the remaining differences matter.

visuals.title: The family tree of the New Testament text
visuals.intro: How the lost originals reach your Bible. Tap a node to see what it is. Families are groups of manuscripts that share characteristic readings.

nodes.label: Original writings
nodes.detail: Paul's letters, the Gospels and the other books as first written, AD 50-95. None survive.

nodes.label: Early papyri
nodes.detail: Second and third century fragments and books such as P52, P46, P66 and P75, mostly from Egypt.

nodes.label: Alexandrian family
nodes.detail: Early, careful text from Egypt: P75, Codex Vaticanus, Codex Sinaiticus. Usually given most weight today.

nodes.label: Western family
nodes.detail: Early but freer text, often expanding or paraphrasing: Codex Bezae and the Old Latin.

nodes.label: Byzantine family
nodes.detail: The text of most later Greek manuscripts and the Greek Orthodox Church. Smoother and fuller; Alexandrinus has it in the Gospels.

nodes.label: Caesarean (doubted)
nodes.detail: Once proposed as a fourth family for the Gospels; many scholars now doubt it is a real group.

nodes.label: Ancient translations
nodes.detail: Latin, Syriac, Coptic and others, made from Greek copies from the second century on. They show which readings existed where.

nodes.label: Church fathers' quotations
nodes.detail: Early teachers quoted Scripture so often that their quotations witness to the text they knew.

nodes.label: Textus Receptus
nodes.detail: Printed Greek texts from Erasmus (1516) to Stephanus and Beza, based on a few late Byzantine manuscripts.

nodes.label: KJV (1611)
nodes.detail: Translated mainly from the Textus Receptus, with the Masoretic Text for the Old Testament.

nodes.label: Critical text
nodes.detail: Nestle-Aland and UBS editions, built by weighing all families, papyri, versions and fathers.

nodes.label: Modern translations
nodes.detail: NIV, ESV, NRSV, NLT, CSB and most new translations, with footnotes where manuscripts differ.

visuals.title: Key manuscripts and editions
visuals.intro: Manuscript dates are estimates from handwriting and materials.

events.label: Great Isaiah Scroll
events.text: The best-preserved Dead Sea Scroll: all 66 chapters of Isaiah.

events.label: P52
events.text: A fragment of John 18, usually dated about 125-175; the oldest known New Testament fragment on most datings.

events.label: P46 and P66
events.text: Most of Paul's letters (P46) and much of John (P66) in papyrus books.

events.label: Codex Vaticanus
events.text: Nearly complete Greek Bible, about 300-350. Kept in the Vatican Library.

events.label: Codex Sinaiticus
events.text: Oldest complete New Testament, about 330-360.

events.label: Codex Alexandrinus
events.text: Early 400s Greek Bible including 1 and 2 Clement; in London since 1627.

events.label: Aleppo Codex
events.text: The finest Masoretic manuscript, partly lost in 1947.

events.label: Leningrad Codex
events.text: Oldest complete Hebrew Bible; basis of modern Hebrew editions.

events.label: Erasmus' Greek New Testament
events.text: The first published printed Greek New Testament, ancestor of the Textus Receptus.

events.label: Sinaiticus found
events.text: Tischendorf sees the first leaves at St Catherine's; he obtains the rest in 1859.

events.label: Westcott and Hort
events.text: A new Greek text based on the oldest manuscripts, used for the Revised Version.

events.label: Dead Sea Scrolls
events.text: Discovery at Qumran pushes the Hebrew evidence back about a thousand years.

events.label: Nestle-Aland 28
events.text: Current standard critical Greek New Testament.

visuals.title: How a textual critic decides
visuals.intro: Walk through the questions scholars ask at a place where manuscripts differ.

steps.label: Gather every witness
steps.detail: List the readings in Greek manuscripts, early translations and church fathers' quotations.

steps.label: Weigh, don't count
steps.detail: Ask how early, how careful and how widespread each reading is. A thousand late copies of one source count as one witness.

steps.label: Explain the others
steps.detail: Which reading best explains how the other readings came about?

steps.label: Think like a scribe
steps.detail: Scribes tended to smooth hard readings, harmonise Gospels and add clarifications. The harder or shorter reading is often older, though not always.

steps.label: Think like the author
steps.detail: Which reading fits the author's own vocabulary, style and argument?

steps.label: Decide and footnote
steps.detail: Print the most likely reading and note serious alternatives so readers can see the evidence.

visuals.title: Does this variant change a doctrine?
visuals.intro: For each real manuscript difference, choose what it affects. Then see the answer and why.

categories.label: Changes a verse, not a doctrine
Touches a practice or debate (no core belief rests on it)

items.text: Some manuscripts read 'Christ Jesus', others 'Jesus Christ'.
items.why: Word-order and naming variants are extremely common and change nothing.

items.text: John's name is spelled with one Greek letter n in some copies and two in others.
items.why: Spelling differences are the largest group of variants and make no difference to meaning.

items.text: 'We have peace with God' or 'Let us have peace with God' (one Greek letter differs).
items.why: It changes the verse from a statement to an encouragement, but peace with God through Christ is taught throughout Romans either way (Rom 5:10-11).

items.text: The KJV's 'the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one'.
items.why: Almost certainly a later Latin addition. The church confessed the Trinity long before it entered Greek printed texts, from passages like Matt 28:19 and 2 Cor 13:14.

items.text: The story of the woman caught in adultery.
items.why: Probably not originally in John, though possibly a true early story. Jesus' mercy to sinners is taught in many undisputed passages (Luke 7:36-50; John 3:17).

items.text: 'Nor the Son' in Jesus' saying that no one knows the day or hour.
items.why: Missing in many later manuscripts of Matthew, but the same words stand undisputed in Mark 13:32.

items.text: 'God was manifest in the flesh' or 'He who was manifested in the flesh'.
items.why: The earlier reading is probably 'He who'. Jesus' deity rests on many other texts (John 1:1; John 20:28).

items.text: The number of the beast is 666 in most copies, 616 in some early ones.
items.why: Irenaeus already knew both. It affects how the number is decoded, not any doctrine.

items.text: Jesus' sweat like drops of blood and the strengthening angel.
items.why: Disputed in early manuscripts. Jesus' anguish in Gethsemane is clear without it (Mark 14:33-36).

items.text: The longer ending of Mark, including picking up snakes and drinking poison.
items.why: Probably not original. A few churches have practised snake-handling from these verses alone, so the variant touches practice, though no core belief depends on it.

items.text: 'For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory for ever' at the end of the Lord's Prayer.
items.why: Absent from the earliest manuscripts; an early liturgical ending (see 1 Chr 29:11). It shapes how churches pray the prayer, not what they believe.

items.text: Women keeping silent: some manuscripts place these verses after verse 40.
items.why: A few scholars, such as Gordon Fee, argue the verses were added; most think they are original but debate their meaning. It feeds a live debate on women's roles, which rests on several passages.

voices.text: There are more variations among our manuscripts than there are words in the New Testament.

views.name: Reasoned eclecticism (the mainstream method)
views.who: Bruce Metzger, Kurt and Barbara Aland, Michael Holmes; the Nestle-Aland and UBS editions
views.summary: At each variant, weigh all the evidence (external: which manuscripts; internal: which reading best explains the others and fits the author) and choose case by case. In practice this often favours the early Alexandrian manuscripts.
views.strengths: It uses all the evidence, including the oldest papyri, and its reasons are published so anyone can check them.
views.critiques: Critics say it relies on a small number of Egyptian manuscripts and on scholars' judgements, which can change. Supporters reply that the judgements are tested against wide evidence and that the results are very stable.

views.name: Byzantine priority (the majority text)
views.who: Maurice Robinson and William Pierpont; earlier Zane Hodges and Arthur Farstad
views.summary: The reading found in the great majority of Greek manuscripts is most likely original, because a text in continuous use across the Greek church would preserve the original best. Early Egyptian copies may be local, unusual forms.
views.strengths: It takes seriously the church's long use of the text and the possibility that early Egyptian survivals are not representative.
views.critiques: Most scholars note that the Byzantine form is not found in the earliest manuscripts and fathers, and that counting copies ignores how many came from the same source.

views.name: Confessional text (Textus Receptus)
views.who: Edward F. Hills, Theodore Letis; many Reformed and KJV-preferring churches
views.summary: God promised to preserve his word (Matt 5:18; Isa 40:8), and he did so through the text the Reformation churches received and used: the Textus Receptus behind the KJV and other Reformation Bibles. Faith, not only historical method, should guide which text the church uses.
views.strengths: It treats preservation as a theological matter and values a stable, received text for worship and memorisation.
views.critiques: Others point out that the TR was made from a few late manuscripts, that its editions differ from each other, and that Erasmus added the Comma Johanneum only in 1522. Defenders reply that providence guided the church's reception. (KJV-only views that treat the English KJV itself as inspired go further and are rejected even by many TR supporters.)

views.name: The 'living text' and sceptical views
views.who: David Parker, *The Living Text of the Gospels*; Bart D. Ehrman
views.summary: Early copying was free enough that the 'original' may be out of reach in some places. Scholars can recover an early 'initial text', but variants also show how early Christians understood and sometimes reshaped their Scriptures.
views.strengths: It is honest about early instability and treats variants as windows into church history.
views.critiques: Others reply that the agreement between P75 and Vaticanus shows strict copying, and that Ehrman himself has said that essential Christian beliefs are not affected by the variants.

misreadings.popular: Some readers, especially in KJV-only circles, say modern Bibles have removed verses such as Acts 8:37, Matt 18:11 and 1 John 5:7, and that this attacks God's word.
misreadings.inContext: These verses are absent from the earliest manuscripts, so the question is whether later copyists added them, not whether modern editors removed them. Modern Bibles usually print them in footnotes or brackets, so nothing is hidden. Scholars such as Bruce Metzger, D. A. Carson (*The King James Version Debate*) and James White explain the evidence.
misreadings.defence: TR and Byzantine-priority supporters answer that the verses stood in the church's Bible for centuries, that God promised to preserve his words (Matt 5:18), and that modern editors rely too much on a few early Egyptian copies. They see 'addition' and 'omission' as an open question in each case.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Believers can lose trust in their Bible, or in other believers, over a misunderstanding of how manuscripts work.

misreadings.topic: The Bible was translated from translation to translation
misreadings.popular: The Bible is like a game of whispers: translated from Hebrew to Greek to Latin to English, changing each time, so we cannot know what it first said.
misreadings.inContext: Modern translations are made directly from Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek texts, built from thousands of manuscripts, some within a century or so of the originals. Errors in copying are real, but because copies spread widely and independently, a mistake in one line of copies can be spotted by comparing others. Scholars such as Peter Gurry and Elijah Hixson (*Myths and Mistakes in New Testament Textual Criticism*) explain this.
misreadings.defence: What the claim gets right: copying did introduce changes, a few of them deliberate, and some places remain uncertain. Even sceptical scholars agree, however, that the text can be recovered to a very high degree.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Knowing how we got the text lets us trust it for the right reasons and handle the footnotes honestly.

discuss: Before this lesson, had you noticed footnotes in your Bible that say 'some manuscripts'? How did they make you feel?
Why might God allow his word to come to us through fallible human copying rather than a perfectly preserved original?
How would you explain to a sceptical friend why the number of variants is not as alarming as it sounds?
The story of the woman caught in adultery is probably not original to John but may well be a true story about Jesus. How should we preach or read it?
What do you think 'God preserves his word' means in light of the manuscript evidence?
practice: Look up Mark 16:8-20 and John 7:53-8:11 in two different Bibles and read their notes or brackets. Write down what each note says.
Visit the Codex Sinaiticus project online and look at a page of the Gospel of John. Notice how the text is written without spaces between words.
Pick one item from the sorter game and explain it to someone in two minutes.
